utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tihic, thank you for coming back. Mr. Milosevic, you want to ask the witness some more questions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly do. This is a very extensive statement, 65 pages.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not really hear Mr. Milosevic. He's speaking without a microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I will try to finish within this first session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You're asking for an hour and a half, are you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. There is some trouble with your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently it wasn't turned towards me. I hope it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In any event, what we'll give you -- we've got to look at the whole time, the time of the case and the time you've had with the witness already. Twenty minutes is what you've got. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot manage to examine within 20 minutes, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tihic, in view of the fact that this statement is much longer and substantial than your statement itself, do you agree that this memoir, as you called it, is much more relevant to the establishment of facts than your statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree. This is -- these are my thoughts and my doubts and dilemmas I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday during your testimony you said you were a member of the SDA since it was founded.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from your notes, we see that it is not true. You hesitated, apparently, a great deal before joining the SDA. On page 3, in paragraph 2, you say: "During the summer and autumn of 1990, it was clear already that national parties would win the elections. I contacted the SDA a lot and I assisted as much as I could in town because many people were illiterate, both politically and literally." Can we say, judging by this paragraph, that you were in doubt, you hesitated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the SDA was established, perhaps two months later, I joined. But before that, I worked a little for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 4, you say that the party was made up mainly of people who were not really prominent or renowned in your community, small businessmen and others and outsiders who moved in recently. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean people who were not originally from Bosanski Samac, who moved in from other places in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly from Bosnia. I believe there was one from Sandzak as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you strengthen this statement and you say: "These outsiders, newcomers, did not know the spirit of Samac and the Muslims and were hard-liners to a greater extent than the locals of Samac."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not a member of the SDA even during the founding session that was held in September 1990 in Bosanski Samac, attended by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your hesitation to join the SDA was strengthened by the differences between Alija Izetbegovic on one hand and Mr. Zulfikarpasic and Muhamed Filipovic on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were my dilemmas that other people shared perhaps as well, when there was a rift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were at the time a friend of Zulfikarpasic and Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you joined the SDA, you spoke of some defence activities of the SDA. How do you explain the fact which you mention on page 7, paragraph 1? You say that in that -- to that end, expert seminars were organised, and you sent people for sabotage training courses.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what went on there, but I know that two or three members, I believe, went to either Doboj or Tesanj, and somebody from Sarajevo came and explained, as far as I know, how these units were established and made plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everybody knows what sabotage training means. You use the term "sabotage training." Were those people responsible for all those sabotage actions on the territory of the municipality I asked you about yesterday and you replied that you didn't know who committed them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We supposed it was the JNA. That means their intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in the same place that you didn't believe in the concept of defence of Doboj imposed by the Regional Centre of the SDA, and you turned towards the HDZ centre in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I realised that these preparations were not really of good quality, and they could not cover Samac, which is 50 kilometres away. And in view of what was going on and the crimes in Bijeljina and elsewhere in Bosnia, we turned more towards the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday you denied the existence of any military structure within the SDA. However, in your notes it says very clearly that you had established a Crisis Staff which you yourself called "command." You used the term "command." And even then it had developed a plan of war. You can see that on page 7 of your notes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said even then that all presidents of municipal organisations of the SDA were simultaneously heads of those Crisis Staffs. They were formally called Crisis Staff, but they were bereft of what Crisis Staffs normally included, because they involved very small numbers of Muslims from town. We accounted for only 7, 8 per cent of the population. It was not enough in terms of structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday. But you say here very clearly: "We simultaneously formed a Crisis Staff." And you used the term precisely "command" and developed the necessary documents such as plan of war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why you don't you read the entirety of that document? We received a document from Sarajevo which specified the things we needed to have. You can establish that and call it command in big places and big municipalities with a large population. You receive papers where it says you should have a command, and we do call it "command," but in reality there is nothing behind it; no manpower, no troops, nothing, no equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you are putting it very differently now. Now we're talking about 1990 and beginning of 1991. Is it indisputable, contrary to your testimony of yesterday, that you were preparing for war? Otherwise, why would you need a plan of war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it didn't happen in 1990. And we were not preparing for war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you had made a plan of war.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not in 1990. It was just before the war itself when we received those instructions which said that we should have a Crisis Staff, a security commission, that this commission should make a defence plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have no time to read everything that is written here, but what you say here is completely different to what is written. When you speak of the person you appointed head of that command for Samac, Alija Fitozovic, to whom referred -- to whom we referred yesterday on a number of occasions, you say - and that is not mentioned in your statement - that he had a drinking problem, that he was an extremist bent towards the Croats. It's all written on page 7.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything is relative, both drinking problems and sympathies for Croats. Everybody, if we're speaking about Muslims, had sympathies for one or the other side. Those who were for the 4th Detachment had sympathies for Serbs. Other people, like Alija Fitozovic, were on the Bosnian side, and that's why he was inclined towards Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you entrusted leadership to a person with a drinking problem.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're saying makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "We accepted explanations regarding Alija Fitozovic who, due to his drinking problem, did not have a really high rating." That is what is written here. And he was a bit of an extremist.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a bit an extremist. That sounds completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We can understand from the text what you really meant. On the same page you say that you then believed that Croats would assist you in case of attack, as was the case in Bosanski Brod, where strong forces of the HV were stationed in Samac -- in Slavonski Brod, sorry.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in case of attack, the Croat side would help us. However, it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did Croat forces take part in the actions in Bosanski Brod?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened in Bosanski Brod. I know they didn't assist us in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you speak about obstruction and failure of Muslims to respond to the reserve forces of the JNA, to join the reserve forces of the JNA, you said yesterday you knew nothing about the appeal made by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say here, I quote: "In keeping with the appeal of Alija Izetbegovic, Muslims, apart from a number of traitors, did not respond to call-ups to do their military service or to join the JNA."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Alija Izetbegovic said we shouldn't go into the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they didn't want to do either their regular military service or to join the reserve.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA attacked Croatia, and in view of everything that happened there, of course we didn't want to take part in the attack on Croatia. We didn't want our boys to die there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no question of that. What you said is that Izetbegovic and everybody who did not comply with his appeal were traitors. Can we establish that much?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did not listen to the legal authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Alija Izetbegovic was then the legal authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it apply to the Muslims only?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It applied to all residents of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some complied, some didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday the 4th Detachment was part of the JNA. It was set up by Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, but here on page 10 of your notes you wrote: "Simo Zaric, without the knowledge of municipal authorities, established the 4th Detachment mainly made up of members of the Serb community and outcasts of the Muslim and Croat communities."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wrote, but Simo Zaric was a reserve officer of the JNA. He was part of the JNA system, and as such he was appointed by Nikolic assistant commander of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this 4th Detachment was indubitably multi-ethnic, made up of Croats, Muslims and Serbs. Right or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly Serbs, and to a lesser extent, Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So there's no doubt that the 4th Detachment was not set up by the JNA. This was not a JNA unit. It was predominantly the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is questionable. That is questionable. It is quite clear that the JNA formed the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then this is some kind of regular unit which goes home. They spent their nights at home. That cannot be a regular JNA unit.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an illegal decision by the JNA, like many others were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you explain who these outcasts of the Muslim people are, you say in the same place that these were people who had no reputation whatsoever, inclined towards crime and bullyish behaviour. There were also a number of Muslims who came from mixed marriages or had wives of Serb ethnicity; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some such persons were there, not all of them, because a large number of them, when they saw what kind of detachment this was, the 4th Detachment, and what kind of JNA this was, then they left it and they joined the HVO units, the BH army, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you say from mixed marriages, married to Serb women and so on, doesn't it seem to you that this is a nationalist view that you took, even a chauvinist position, if I may say so?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. Because usually these persons -- I mean, for these persons Yugoslavia was the only solution. Many Muslims had already opted for Yugoslavia. They trusted the Yugoslav People's Army. And particularly these people from mixed marriages. They were for the most part inclined towards that and they were less critical, and they had more trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From that point of view, Fadil Topcagic, Avdo Dzuheric, and Nijaz Ramusovic are three Muslims you call the greatest enemies of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I put it that way, that they were the greatest enemies of the Muslim people. No, no, certainly not. They did make a mistake in joining the 4th Detachment. They shouldn't have done that. But that they are the greatest enemies, I mean, one has to do something more in order to become the greatest enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say all members of the detachment were armed and kept their weapons at home.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of these people were in contact with us as well, and they said that they got a mortar from the JNA or a machine-gun or something like that, because some of them joined us later, together with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this could not have been the regular army if they went home and if they kept their weapons at home. And what you're denying now, that you did not use this expression, I'm going to read this out to you: "These three members of the Muslim people were our greatest enemies." That is what you wrote yourself.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see what the JNA was like. They gave weapons to people to keep them at home. The Serbs got these weapons a year before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that's the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence does take their equipment home, and they sleep at home. This cannot be JNA units. JNA units are in barracks.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is not the Territorial Defence, not in the system of Territorial Defence. Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic was commander of that unit together with those who he had appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that the 4th Detachment had the support of the JNA, isn't that a clear indicator that what you stated yesterday was incorrect? Because why would this be support if they were part of the JNA? Then they would be acting as the JNA, not as the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the 17th Tactical Group. That is what Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic said. And it wasn't only the 4th Detachment of Bosanski Samac. It is a fact that there was another detachment in Crkvina, in a village near Bosanski Samac. This was an entire system, the 17th Tactical Group, whose commander was Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that you were trying to avoid a conflict with them and you mentioned the reasons for that, and also you say that you were working on the disintegration of the 4th Detachment. How were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the inside. We were trying to persuade the people who had joined the 4th Detachment that they did not belong there, and part of them gave us information about arms and meetings and so on, and some of them crossed over to our side and were then detained as soon as they took Samac. There were people there who trusted the JNA, who believed in Yugoslavia, and who were disillusioned when they realised what this was all about, when they realised that this was not the Yugoslav People's Army, that it was a Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tihic. One of the ways in which it can be broken up is the description you gave on page 10, but yesterday you did not make any reference to that. I'm quoting you: "We were spreading rumours, publishing secret pamphlets -- leaflets and naming the Muslims who had joined the detachment, and we call them domestic traitors, and we included people like Esad Delic who were not even a member of the 4th Detachment. In this way, we wanted to prevent other people from joining the detachment. We said that we had nothing to do with the leaflet but people knew that it was us." These are your words authentically. Is that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the only unit that is multi-ethnic, and you tried to disintegrate it, to break it up, and you even published secret leaflets, and you are trying to say that people who were not members of the unit were.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way it was, but this unit -- this detachment was part of the project to destroy Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was joined by some people who were deluded, and we wanted to explain things to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you spread these leaflets against them, these secret leaflets against them in order to discredit them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are they secret?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what is written in your text. I'm just reading your words. And you said that you had nothing to do with these leaflets, that it had nothing to do with you and so on. And then there were threats, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no threats. And of course one disavows something if one does not sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, your last question, Mr. Milosevic. You've had your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know, Mr. May, how to put a question to Mr. Tihic if you won't give me any time at all. This is 65 pages, a 65-page statement, Mr. May. How can you give me 20 minutes only?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you want to ask another question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to ask a few more questions unless you turn off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You were given 20 minutes, Mr. Milosevic. Now, it's a matter for you; do you want to ask him one more question or not? We'll go on to re-examination if not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, on page 15 you say the attack on Samac was not expected. You did not expect it because on the other side of the Sava River were these forces as well as the Green Berets that on several occasions crossed the bridge, and you say that they disarmed the Serbs. So your forces were there together with the Croat forces. Is that right, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not right. You take things out of context and from different parts of my memoir and then you twist it. We were expecting a JNA attack but we were sort of hoping it wouldn't happen. And we were trying to avoid it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one more thing, Mr. Tihic. You said yesterday when I asked you about different occasions when you organised the shipment of weapons. I put -- you said that I was putting the same question to you five times.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in your memoir, you give six examples of different situations in which you bring in weapons, and you even say that you yourself gave instructions for this. The first example is 100 kilogrammes of explosives and then 10.000 bullets, and then mines and grenades. And then the third example, 30 automatic rifles and five pistols. And then Sead Memic, who also drove weapons. Then also on page 14, you have yet another 50 rifles, mortars, Zoljas, ammunition, and so on. So you gave more examples than I did in your memoir, and yesterday you said to me that I keep quoting the same example to you five times.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. You keep repeating one and the same thing twice. Even now, Sead Memic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But please let us clarify this. Please look at page 12, paragraph 1. You said: "We said that we were not opposed to having the JNA in Crkvina, because ultimately it is already there in accordance with the agreement between the republican MUP and the so-called JNA. While we were opposed to their stationing in Uzarija. As a reason, we mentioned the reaction of the Croat side which could cross -- which could close the bridge, and that is Bosnia's only outlet to Europe." I'm quoting you. I'm not drawing on any conclusions. "The real reason was because we knew that ours were transported to Bosnia across this bridge. So a checkpoint by Uzarija would stop the import of weapons." Do you have any comment to make with regard to the assertion you made here which you totally denied yesterday but I'm quoting you right now, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, you destroyed all the bridges on the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some weapons came across the bridge on the Sava River, and in comparison to what you distributed to only one ethnic group in Bosnia, this was nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you want to exhibit this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Any objection to that Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll get the next D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 222, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we have this document and we read it. We don't propose to allow any more cross-examination on it. It was for the accused that the extra time was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the fact that the document is now in evidence, I have no further questions. I will rely on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Mr. Tihic, thank you for coming back, and you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to call Mr. Ahmet Zulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for him, we may as well get a new number for the exhibit bundle.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 609, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I also give to the Court and also to the accused and the amici just a brief note which the accused [sic] wanted to put before the Court concerning a slight correction he wanted to make in his statement which he only was able to tell us last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, when he comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You said the accused wanted to put the statement before the Court. I rather doubt that. No doubt the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you for your correction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, you made a few corrections to your statement yesterday. We'll kindly show you a piece of paper and you can confirm that those corrections were indeed made by yourself.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And may I ask that this be placed before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have it. It should be probably exhibited. It may be convenient to make it part of Exhibit 609, give it a tab number in 609.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 12, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, have you already given evidence before this Tribunal on the 7th, 17th and 18th of June 2002, in the case of the Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And it is that evidence, Your Honour, which has been exhibited, with associated exhibits, before this Tribunal. Thank you. Now, this witness is from Sanski Most municipality in Bosnia, and he is a 92 bis (D) witness, so I shall briefly summarise very quickly the essence of his evidence. He was born and grew up in Sanski Most where he also worked, and in 1991 when the war in Croatia was starting, there was a great deal of nationalist propaganda on the radio. The JNA started to set up barricades and search vehicles, and it was only the Muslim vehicles that were searched. The SDS, in April, wanted to divide the municipality into two parts, a Serbian part and a Muslim part. However, the SDA party were not agreeable. Then followed various paramilitary groups, including the White Eagles from Serbia, coming into Sanski Most. On the 13th of May, the Serb army attacked the village of Trnovo with mortars and anti-aircraft cannons, and on the 14th of May, the Serbs attacked Sanski Most police station which had already been divided. The witness heard these explosions. The Muslim population were then required to surrender all their weapons, which they did, at least most of them. And then on 27th of May, 1992, the inhabitants of the village of Mahala were gathered in the local soccer stadium. On the 28th of May, the Serb artillery shelled Mahala. There was no resistance because that suburb of Sanski Most was empty, the inhabitants being already in the soccer stadium. After that, some of the houses were set on fire and the village was looted. This was witnessed by Mr. Zulic. On the 18th of June Mr. Zulic was arrested and taken to the Betonirka factory, which became a detention facility. It consisted of three small garages and there were 30 people in this garage. There was not enough room, it was too hot, and they were regularly beaten by the guards. On one occasion, on the 22nd of June, the witness was taken out of the garage and was taken by car to a place called Kriva Cesta where he was given a hoe and ordered to join about 20 to 25 other men and to start digging his grave. Whilst at a picnic table about a hundred metres away the witness saw the then-president of the SDS, Mr. Rasula, with other officials and also Serbs wearing JNA uniforms. All of the men except three were slaughtered. The witness however, had a pistol put in his mouth, had some teeth knocked out, but was taken back to Betonirka detention facility. On the 7th of July he was transported to Manjaca camp. Before getting on the truck the detainees were all again severely beaten. Inside the truck, again, it was overcrowded, it was extremely hot, there was no water hardly, and despite their shouts for assistance, a number of the people in the truck died. They were not given any assistance. A young man of 18 died in the witness's lap. On reaching Manjaca, when the witness got out of the truck, there were about 18 to 20 people lying in the truck, most of them motionless. About six of these showed some signs of life but a doctor examined them and they were put back on the truck because the camp commander didn't want them because they were dying. Whilst in Manjaca, the witness was held in a stable with other detainees. The food was inadequate. He was severely beaten, as were most of the other detainees, and he also witnessed at least two of the detainees being killed. After such beatings, often the witness would fall unconscious. The beatings were carried out by guards, and he suffered broken ribs and injuries to his head. He was eventually released from Manjaca on 24th, 25th November, 1992, with his weight having been reduced from 90 kilos to 55 kilos. Now, that is the essence of this witness's evidence, which is also before you in his transcripts together with a number of exhibits which include diaries which were made by the witness and set out in far further detail actually what happened to him and the conditions in which he was detained, and that ends my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One hour for cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic, if you require it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zulic, you made and signed two statements, the first on the 24th of May, 2000, which is shorter and which you made to the authorities in Bosnia; and the second, considerably longer, you made on the 15th and 16th of February and on the 14th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you telling the truth in both statements?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which statement did you tell the truth and which didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I didn't tell the truth in any of them. If Their Honours will close the session for the public, I will explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zulic. We have established then that you were not telling the truth in both statements, but let us see what, in fact, can be clarified. I hope you will assist. Tell me, please, what was the composition of the population in the Sanski Most municipality before the war?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: To tell the truth, I can't be precise, but I do know that there were about -- that there were about 2 or 3 per cent more Muslims than Serbs in Sanski Most. Whether it was 2, 3, or 5 per cent, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not insisting on precise data. At the elections in 1990, the Serbian Democratic Party won the elections. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the president of the municipality was Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And right after the SDS was the SDA; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the deputy, Mirzet Karabeg, the deputy mayor, was from the SDA.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who does Sanski Most belong to now; the federation or Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Serbs are there now in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have information as to how many Serbs fled from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I'm not a politician. I'm not interested in this. I was not active in politics either before the war or after the war, Your Honours. I'm not interested in this. I know that very few Serbs have come back, but I'm not a politician, and I don't keep statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbs were expelled from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't expelled. They fled. Those are two different things. To be expelled and to flee, those are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zulic. We won't go into these nuances as to whether they were expelled or whether they fled because their lives were threatened. Let's leave that aside now. Tell me, please, you say that you were not active in politics, and I respect that, but on page 1, the last paragraph, and on the third page of your statement of 2001, you say: "I noticed the first changes in the municipality when the war in Croatia began. For example, I heard some miners, Serbs who were coming back from the front in Croatia, as they said, and who said that the Muslims would have problems when the war started."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I heard, because I was a shift leader -- don't interrupt me; I don't interrupt you. I was a shift leader in the mine, and as we went to the mine by bus, I was actually foreman under the ground, and I was able to visit every part of the mine. And people split into groups, and those who were called up for regular military exercises went to Croatia, and they received their salaries. I was able to have access to them and to hear what they were saying, and of course these were changes that took place, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm sorry if you think I interrupted you. I wasn't interrupting you, I hadn't completed my question. I was quoting you. And three sentences further on, only three sentences further on, you say: "In June 1991, I remember telling my friends that the Muslims were expecting terrible things to happen." This was in June when the war hadn't even started in Slovenia let alone in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Have you finished your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what did you conclude this?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I concluded this -- I'll tell you the names. Todor Bilbija -- let me just remember the other man's name from Koprina [phoen]. Lazo Damjanovic, Mile Apac. The three of them were standing there in a corridor near the rubber conveyer belt underground, and they were saying that they were going for military exercises, and they said that everything that bore the Muslim name would vanish. I said to them, "But we're working here together." And they said, "No, we know what we know, and you do your job."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zulic. So you concluded that the Muslims would have problems when the war began before any war had broken out.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you discussed the problems that the Muslims would have at a time when no one could have come back from the front in Croatia, when you couldn't have heard about this from Serbs. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They were already going for military exercises. And when they came back, they would gather together as I have just explained. They went for military exercises, and they talked, and I overheard their conversations, and I told them what I've just said. I said, "Men, don't you see that we're working here, working together?" And they said, "You mind your business and we'll mind ours." Your Honours, if anyone is intelligent, they can understand. I heard this with my own ears. Todor Bilbija, Lazo Damjanovic, and Mile whose last name I can't remember but we all called him Japa, they said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zulic. Please don't go into these details, and don't tell us the names of people standing by the conveyer belt in the mine, because this is a waste of time. Let me just ask you: According to your statement of 2001, you saw the first checkpoint in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, everybody was stopped. No differences were made. This is what it says in your statement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Agha just said that only Muslims were searched. What is true?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think that the gentleman mistook the year. I think that it says in my statement that starting in March 1992, it was only Muslims who were searched, and I think it says in my statement that starting in 1991, when the first checkpoints were set up in 1991, that's how it was. And in 1992, starting in March or April -- I can't remember because 12 years have elapsed, but since -- after that time, only Muslims were searched, only non-Serbs, that is, Croats and Muslims. I know because I sometimes went to work by car, and my car was regularly searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that Serb cars were not searched, and how would they know which car was Serb and which was Muslim? The cars did not have any signs on them.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. You could see on one's driving licence what ethnicity they were. They would stop people, check them. And Sanski Most was so small that we all practically knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In September you saw the first checkpoint. At that time, everybody was checked without distinction, and you heard about the arming of the Serbs the eve of Bajram 1992, from Erevin Bajramovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think it's Elmin Nadarevic. And we left work early for Bajram. We were in the second shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you but there's no need to explain what shift you were on. All I'm trying to establish is this: The first checkpoint you saw was in September 1991 when everybody was checked, and on the eve of Bajram 1992, you heard from this colleague of yours that Serbs were arming. So you say so both of these phenomena, the checkpoints in 1991 and what your colleague told you in 1992 on the eve of Bajram, this could not be the basis of the allegation you made that the Muslims were expecting terrible things to happen, because you learned about this several months after June 1991. Both of these things happened much later and couldn't have prompted your expectations.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: First of all, you did interrupt me, and secondly, I have to expand because you're putting lengthy questions to me, because if I don't explain everything, you ask the same question again. I wanted to explain, for example, that I think this man's name was not Bajramovic but Nadarevic. I think it's a mistake in the translation. And secondly, he got back to the car -- he got into my car and he said, "Please, I can't pass through here. Put me in the car and drive me home taking a roundabout route." He said, "The army is distributing weapons here. Who are they distributing the weapons to? Serbs." I said, "Well, let's join the queue and get weapons too." I'm just saying what I said. But we did go around and I saw a military truck parked there and people coming and taking weapons from it. I saw this with my own eyes together with this other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. Zulic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From your statement from 2001, it follows from the last two paragraphs on page 3 that most Serb soldiers in Sanski Most were local Serbs, as you say.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That was the SOS, the Serbian armed forces, SOS. I think it should state that somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you is it correct that most of these forces were made up of local people, local Serbs, as you say?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Most of them, yes. In the town, yes. The ones manning the checkpoints, the ones driving around by car -- by truck, Nunja, Medeni Saovic. Medeni, that was his nickname, I really don't know his name. Nunja was a driver in my company. Medeni was a mechanic. They were the leaders of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They were your colleagues from work.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then you say that in May 1992, and that is the last paragraph on page 3, you noticed that many different units were passing through the municipality. What were those units? Were they passing on a road that units were using?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Right below my village - my village is called Pobrijezje, and it is called Pobrijezje because it's in the foot of a hill or on the slope of a hill - there is a road, so you can see well when units are passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were they going, in which direction?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Some of them were going in the direction of Lusci Palanka and Bosanska Krupa. Others were going towards a hill called Dzedovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they also local units, the Territorial Defence, something like that? What were they? Were they paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: In those units, there were lorries -- not only lorries but tanks and those armoured vehicles with a gun turret on top. There wore JNA emblems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You speak of various paramilitary units. You mention White Eagles and then you use the term "Seselj's men," and you say they were coming from all parts of the country, dressed in olive drab grey uniforms. How did you establish that they were White Eagles or Seselj's men, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, White Eagles wore those white ribbons on the left arm, as far as I remember, and Seselj's men wore fur-lined hats with cockades, and they wore long beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that a paramilitary unit or what?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think they were paramilitaries. How could I know? I know they had weapons. I know what they looked like. But whether they were regular troops, irregular troops or paramilitaries, I have no idea. I didn't put those emblems on them, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm asking. How can you know that some of them were Seselj's men? According to my information, they only joined the JNA or the Territorial Defence as volunteers. They didn't have units of their own. Did you see a unit of Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Their unit was stationed on a cemetery where Partisans from World War II are buried. It's called Milen Birit [phoen]. One of them was a local resident, because whenever these paramilitary units came, they would recruit a couple of local men. And I know one of these locals. He was a digger in the mine. I can't remember his name right now. I saw this man on one occasion and I was very surprised to see that he had a cockade on his headgear. His name is Milo. If you give me a second, I will remember his name. Uros Boranovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In a transcript I'm reading from your testimony in the Brdjanin and Talic case, page ending with number 6856, lines 4 to 8, it seems to follow that White Eagles and Seselj's men are one and the same thing. I think you must be confused in your mind, and that's what you said in response to a question from this bogus Prosecution. Could you tell me just one thing: Are these two different groups or one and the same?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They're all the same to me. He came to our town to kill Muslims, and to me it's all the same whether he's an Arkan's man or Seselj's man or a White Eagle. They didn't like Muslims, obviously. If they did, we would have met them with flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zulic. As to how these conflicts began, there is enough information available. I will only stick to your statement. On -- towards the end of page 3 of this statement from year 2000 you say that: "I know that Rasula --" that's the man who became president of the municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I continue: "I know that Rasula and these SOS men met behind the cafe called United Brothers, owned by Mustafa. I know this because Muhamed Karabeg, who was a maintenance man in my mine, had a shop behind this location and he told me that Rasula and other members of the War Presidency regularly meet with SOS men and with Mr. Saovic, who is commander of the SOS men." Now, tell me, don't you think it doesn't make any sense at all to conceive that the president of the municipality and members of the War Presidency, that is to say the authorities who have their own offices, would meet behind some cafe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I have to clarify this, Your Honours. Since one of the Krunic brothers - whether it was Buco or Milorad, I don't know - owned a cafe a little bit to the front and the other had a cafe behind, they would meet there. So when they were organising parties, dinners, festivities, they would do it in the second cafe behind the first cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that to say that they sat together in a coffee bar having dinner or drinks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw them having dinner or lunch together or something like that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I didn't. Muhamed did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Muhamed did. Now --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: But look, I saw them once when I was bringing material. And I'm sorry I'm interrupting you. I brought some material because he had asked me to. That material was some progress report for work. And I saw this drinking party with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw him sitting in a cafe and drinking and eating, but that's not what I'm asking you about. From your statement, pages 5 and 6, it follows that in the second half of May 1992, you went to the mine to collect your salary, and you saw with your own eyes members of the War Presidency meeting outside of the Slozna Braca cafe, and you named them, Rasa, Zjenic [phoen], Tripkovic, Maric, and others. You knew about these meetings from the stories of Muhamed Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I submitted my report, I collected my salary, and that's what I wanted to ask you. Just ask me your questions so we save time for your own sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you name on one of the pages the members of the War Presidency, and you say that Boro Tadic, who was a friend of yours, was in the War Presidency, in charge of the SOS. You say: "I would see him coming to those meetings."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. If -- and this is my question: If you knew about these meetings from the stories of Muhamed Karabeg apart from that one case when you saw them gathering outside the cafe with the exception of Boro Tadic, how can you say that you would see Boro Tadic coming to the meetings?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No. I saw him that once. Maybe it's a translation mistake. Maybe the translator said "meetings" and I said "meeting." It could be an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the penultimate paragraph on page 4, statement of 2000, you say that in April you bought a machine-gun from a Serb for your own personal protection.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that a bit too much, to buy a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Have you completed your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did it ever occur to you to buy a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I went to this cafe with my nephews, and this Serb took me aside and said, "Come on, buy this. You'll need it." I paid him 500 deutschmark for it. He chipped in 20 rounds. And if you ask me how it ever occurred to me, of course it occurred to me. I had a family to think of. Of course, if life had been normal, if everything had been as usual, of course I would have never bought it. And for many years, withdrawals were made from my salary to finance the JNA. And the same goes for all the Muslims. We armed the JNA, and they took and distributed weapons to only one ethnic group. If they had been a real army, they would have either disarmed all ethnic groups or distributed weapons to all ethnic groups, and then there would have been no bloodshed. But it's true. They did distribute weapons to one ethnic group. And it was, I think, some sort of foul play because you might say that 500 deutschmark was very little to pay for a machine-gun, but that's how things were at the time. And I think it was a set-up, because people who later came to look for a weapon in my house had the serial number of my gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say you threw it later into a well in your village?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not because you gave up the idea of defending your family but because you thought it might have been a set-up; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand now. Because I found it difficult to understand earlier when you say that the Serbs later interrogated you about this purchase, "And I kept denying that I had ever bought a gun, otherwise they would have killed me for sure." If they knew you had a machine-gun, and they probably didn't since they were only questioning you, and moreover, if you had been set up by them, wouldn't you think that denying it was more dangerous than just confirming something they knew anyway, all the more so because you never used that machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, that's exactly the crux of the matter. That's the reason why I didn't turn over my gun, because all those who did were killed. They're dead now. Anybody who had a weapon of any kind is dead now. They're not among the living any more. Anybody who ever surrendered a weapon, even a sporting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any sense in what you're saying? I can't understand how somebody could have been killed just because they turned over a hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I can tell you the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm not asking you about the names, I'm just trying to fit facts together. I don't know the names even if you told them. But does it make any sense at all that somebody would be killed just because they responded to an appeal and turned over the gun to the police?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I would have to take some time to explain this. I know about my village. I made those -- I made a picture in my head. I have an understanding. Teufik Camber [phoen] turned over a sporting rifle at the time. He's now dead. Idriz Karabeg was killed that same year after turning over a hunting rifle. Mr. Omic also turned over the same gun and was killed. Another man I know turned over an army rifle and was killed. It wasn't difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zulic. On page 4 you say: "I have never been a member of organised or unorganised resistance. I know people who wanted to organise some sort of resistance, but nobody actually did it." And already on the next page, on page 5, in the paragraph which begins with the words, "On the 13th of May, 1992 ..." you say: "In our patrols in Pobrijezje, we were still using hunting weapons and our own rifles." So after all, you did conduct some armed activities.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only quoting you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, you can continue to quote me. We agreed with people from the next village, with Serbs, to have guards organised, not patrols. I think you are misquoting me. I could not have said that. All I said was we had a meeting with the Serbs, not only Pobrijezje but also villages of Sehovci, Trnova, and Podlug. And we agreed at this meeting to have joint guards with Serbs. However, when we came actually there to stand guard to Podlug, the Serbs said you stand your own guard and we'll stand our own. So Serbs wanted to have their own Serb guards and Muslims wanted to have -- Muslims were told to keep their own guards. So it was not a military organisation of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is beyond dispute that you had weapons.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I did have a hunting weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those were not unarmed guards or guard posts. You were using the guns you had.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: So were the Serbs. They were not unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not even saying that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I am saying that. I saw it with my own eyes. They put up a guard post outside the house of Aco Veselinovic. They put up those iron grills, sandbags, and machine-gun nest. And when we came to join them, as agreed, they said, "No. You keep your own guards." I'm telling you what I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I understand you full well. My question only referred to this quotation from page 5 where you said: "In our patrols in Pobrijezje, we were still using hunting weapons and our own rifles." So at any rate, you were armed, as I want to establish because you previously said you were unarmed, having turned over all your weapons previously.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, something doesn't sound right here. Wait a minute. Somewhere in my statement that I gave to the investigators you should be able to find a place where I said that guards stopped after weapons were turned over. Dragan Adzic, son of Slavo Adzic, came and picked up all our weapons. From that time on, there were no more guard posts. So those are two different things. One thing is your interpretation, and the other thing is reality. You want to represent me as saying that we had weapons throughout that time. You may be a better reader than I am, I have only the secondary school, but if you are careful and if you read carefully, you find that; I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zulic, but please bear in mind the fact that I'm just quoting your statement. I really don't have any other information except for your own statement. That is why I'm asking for an explanation, because I quoted to you what is written over here. But let us move on. In the second paragraph on page 5, before the sentence on patrols, so before the sentence on patrols, it says, and I'm reading out from your statement exactly the way it's been written, I'm quoting you: "Until then --" and that is the 13th of May, 1992 -- "until -- by this time, Muslims and Croats had to return the former JNA uniforms and any private weapons in their possession. Also, the weapons that Muslims and Croats were issued in the TO were seized, that the TO had given them."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Muslims and Croats had not acted in accordance with that order because, according to what you said, they had their own patrols and they had guard duty; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I explained this the first time in relation to the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: After the 13th of May, after this was taken away -- well, it wasn't taken away. Your Honour, I have to go on for a while. I do apologise, but I have to explain some things. These weapons were not seized in the sense of them going from one house to the other. Quite simply, over the radio they said Muslims and Croats -- this is quite literally what they said: "Muslims and Croats, hand over your weapons. The Serb authorities guarantee your safety and security as well as that of your property." That was over the radio. And immediately over the radio they said, for example in the case of Pobrijezje, that this would be by the social centre in the village of Pobrijezje, that military personnel would come there and they would take these weapons. And people did bring the weapons in. And that is why I threw my weapon away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zulic. On the 13th of May you did that, and from the 13th of May onwards you didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No one in the village had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 5 you say: "On the 13th of May, I saw Serbs leaving in military trucks for the mountains. I saw that they had their families with them, with tractors. They left behind those Serbs who had not yet made up their minds and threatened them because they had not put on their uniforms." That is a quotation from your statement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, isn't it pointless for Serbs, who are in charge of the authorities in the government there and who, in your opinion, have Sanski Most under their control, and there in Sanski Most, in your own words there are no Muslim or Croat armed forces and there are no operations, they are fleeing with tractors into the mountains. Why were they fleeing into the mountains? I've quoted you just now.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Correct, you've quoted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With tractors, their families going into the mountains.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I have.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, that is pointless, right, but there seems to be something different involved there, a different example altogether. Since the town had a mixed population, Mahala and Muhici were, say, 90 per cent Muslim, and the remaining 10 per cent were Serbs and Croats. Now, since Sanski Most was supposed to be targeted from the hills, was there the possibility of a shell straying into a neighbourhood where there was a Serb majority? That was the reason. Because Zeljko Srbac, an engineer from the mine, said -- and I'm sorry I'm using an expletive now when I quote, I'm quoting what Zeljko said, "Oh, fuck they left me and my family just because I didn't want to get dressed, and they took everything." Because I asked him why they were going into the mountains. Are you happy with this answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't ask the accused if he's happy with the answer. He'd better be. He can ask you some further questions. But you've only got a quarter of an hour left, Mr. Milosevic. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes. Mr. Zulic, I must tell you, as we tell all witnesses, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, could you please explain something to me. This witness is testifying on the basis of your Rule 92 bis, that is to say without examination-in-chief. The basis for my cross-examination are the statements that were provided to me. But then the witness said that they are not correct, these statements. So I assume that you should give me some time to establish what in actual fact did happen over there. Otherwise, I do not see how I can carry out a cross-examination on the basis of the statements that the witness himself said were incorrect. He admitted that they were incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The documents which were admitted are in the bundle of Exhibit 609, and the document which has been admitted is the transcript of his testimony in Brdjanin together with several other exhibits which aren't statements or anything connected with it. So no statement has been admitted. We have got an addendum in which he clarifies something, but at the moment, his statements aren't admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. I don't believe, actually, the witness has said that his statement which he gave the ICTY is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, no doubt that's something you can clarify in due course, Mr. Agha. Yes. If you want to ask any further questions about the statements, which are not in evidence at the moment, if you want to ask any further questions about them, you can, but bear in mind you may have to go into private session to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May, but do I have the time now for questioning this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you move on with it, we'll see. There's a limit to the time you can have, as you know, with any witness. We'll see what use you make of the quarter of an hour which remains for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Zulic, in your statement of 2001, you said that on the 14th of May, over the radio, you heard that the Serb forces had attacked the Muslim police station located in Sanski Most, and that after it was divided, the police station, that it was in the basement and that you personally heard explosions around 2200 hours in the evening.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these explosions a result of the attack on the police station?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If there were explosions, that means that some kind of heavy weaponry was used. How is it possible for someone to attack the basement of the municipality with some kind of heavy weaponry without damaging in any way the municipality building itself? Because it was the SDS that held the municipal authorities in its own hands in that building.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Not then. At that time, the municipality was empty. After the municipality was divided, the Yugoslav People's Army was there too. On the 18th of April, the Yugoslav People's Army blocked the town, and it was announced over the radio that the town would be divided into the Serb and Muslim sections. The army stood by the bridge on the Sana River and in front of the police station and in the square while they held a meeting at the municipality building on that day. I know that because I went for the memorial service of Hamil Asic [phoen], a relative of mine, and we could not get from the mosque to the cemetery. We had to walk all the way around town. Then we had to pass by the police station in order to get to the Greda cemetery. And I saw a military vehicle there in front of the police station at the crossroads where the road to Greda is as well as the road leading to the centre of town. The mosque is on the other side of the bridge, so I saw this on the other side of the bridge. And when they divided the town, they said that the Muslims had control of the municipality building, whereas the Serbs had control of the police station, the Kljucka Street, and I cannot remember everything else now, how it was divided exactly. It's been almost 12 years now -- no, almost 13 years now since that division, but I know that it was roughly along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In relation to the attack on the SUP, the members of the Muslim SUP, did they offer any resistance or not?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if they did not offer any resistance, why would anybody use weapons to attack someone who was not resisting? And with heavy weaponry at that, because you heard an explosion.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, look: My assumption is, and you will have to ask those who did the attacking, but my assumption is that this had the intention of expelling the Muslims from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zulic. On page 2, in paragraph 2 -- let us try to deal with this as fast as possible -- you mention your diary that you kept in Manjaca from the 15th of July, 1992, onwards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think it was from the 28th of August that I started keeping not a diary but simply started jotting things down in a pad that I got from a Serb from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you got this in a package that this Serb friend of yours sent to you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So people were allowed to receive parcels at the camp in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: From the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When arriving in another country, as you said in the same paragraph, you copied your diary in three new notebooks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, what happened to the original notes that you wrote down in this writing pad that you got in the parcel from your friend?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I have them. I mean, what notes do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The original notes that you made in that writing pad in camp, because you say that you copied this in three new notebooks. What happened to the original writings?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I have the original. Here it is. And, Your Honours, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not hand it in, so it cannot be seen?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I handed in copies and copies exist. That is in the transcript, that I handed in copies of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, will you help us, please. Is this -- we have a handwritten text attached to the exhibits, Exhibit 609, tab 3. Is that the document to which we're referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes. This ought to be his handwritten diary which was exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, let's go on. Thank you very much. No need to hand it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you submit a copy of precisely that piece of paper that you're holding in your hands now or what you wrote down in these three notebooks later?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Copies of this and copies of the three notebooks too. I handed in all these copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I did not receive a copy of that or of the three notebooks. Tell me, in these notebooks in which you copied these notes, did you refer to events that took place before the 15th?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So even before you started keeping this diary as of the 28th of August, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of my memory, as far as I could remember. I started keeping it sometime from the village of Ravno, when the village of Ravno was levelled. And then through Bijeljina, Sarajevo, I just briefly wrote down how things went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In this same paragraph you say that your diary is a lengthy one and that it includes information that is not contained in your statement. At the same time, you say that your statement contains things that do not exist in the diary. So what is this all about?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think that you're putting the wrong questions to me or that you're trying to say something wrong. First of all, I stand by what I said to the Judges, that my diary is the way it is. It doesn't even contain 10 per cent of all the things that happened to me and that happened in Sanski Most. That is the first thing I wish to say. The second thing I wish to say is I did not want to write down many things in these -- this diary, because when this diary was written, nobody knew anything about The Hague. I did not think that I was writing it for the public. I wrote on the first page of this diary "Lest our grandchildren forget." So there are many things I did not write down, because I wanted -- I did not want my grandchildren to know everything that I had gone through, Your Honours, because there would be even more hatred in their hearts if they knew everything that had happened. Mr. Milosevic insists on quoting only one thing, I mean, why I did not want to say everything, but could we please move into private session now so that I could tell you at least part of this, just one little part of what I experienced and why I did not write it down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, my question was related only to a quotation from your statement, where you say: "My diary is a lengthy one and it contains details that are not in my statement, and the statement contains things that I eyewitnessed and are not contained in my diary."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it says that my diary is a lengthy one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading what it says here. "My diary is a lengthy one, and it contains details that are not in my statement." I'm reading this from page 2 of your statement. Basically it is the first page of your statement, but it is marked as page 2 of your witness statement. This is the one but last sentence in your second paragraph. So it says: My diary is lengthy and contains details that are not in my statement, and my statement contains items that I witnessed and that are not in my diary." I read the whole sentence to you, from the first capital letter up to the full stop at the end. I have no other basis for putting questions to you except for your own statement, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: It is true that that is what it says here, but if you look at this, it should not have been the word used, "lengthy," no, because the day before yesterday, when I was with the Prosecutor, I said that only this much was written in my diary. And probably as I was reading this, I skipped that. However, in the transcript from the last trial, there is what I said exactly in the transcript when I testified the last time, that my diary is this big, just -- just so that my grandchildren would not forget, and that I did not explain anything in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zulic. In paragraph 1 on page 14, you say that on the 29th of August, when you arrived in Manjaca, you stopped taking notes in your diary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, in the case that I mentioned for you, Mr. May, here, and then I'm giving you the exact case number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that this is being read out too fast, they cannot keep up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to read, read fairly slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says, and it was established by your own decision or the decision taken by your colleagues, that this was some kind of a fact, that 1.464 persons from Prijedor were taken to Manjaca on the 6th of August, 1992. You are talking about prisoners of the 29th of August, that they arrived from Prijedor then, and that is when you stopped keeping a diary altogether, whereas in this other case the date mentioned is the 6th of August. Which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: It is correct that it was the 19th. The 19th of August is fair day in Sanski Most, and that is when they made a promise to us. People were saying that the Manjaca camp would be dissolved and that they'd send buses to drive us away. They did not come on the 6th. On the 29th of August, though, prisoners came from the municipality of Sanski Most, those who had been taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But then on the basis of this, what was part of the decision that pertains to the 6th of August is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were an eyewitness. You said on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know, because the 19th of August was the day when the fair was held in Sanski Most. In the evening, these buses came and we did not know how many of them were there or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
