utterances.text: All right. Just tell me one thing: For how long did you keep this diary? From which date until which date? Can that be established?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: At this moment, I'm telling you I kept a diary until sometime in the end of August. Your Honours, I'll explain this. I started writing this diary in this very small writing pad, and that is where I recorded the events in Sanski Most, and there is the date on the back too. And then when I came to Cologne in Germany, I went for Christmas, around Christmastime, and we had nothing to do, so I took this diary and I started writing. I started writing from the village of Ravno onwards, to the best of my memory. And I wrote until the end of August. When I left the barracks in Cologne, I got a job and I had no more time to write in my notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you wrote that in Cologne?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was written in Cologne, from Christmas 1992 until the end of January, approximately, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, in Zulic. On page 3, paragraph 1, you say that the Muslims and Croats who refused to go to the front line were dismissed from their jobs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that the factory called Splonum [phoen] - I assume that is a brick factory - worked at full capacity and that nobody was dismissed. As a matter of fact, in the autumn of 1991 there were many more Muslims employed there rather than Serbs.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, people who were in management positions were dismissed, but the Muslims who were manual labourers were kept there in order to work. But the managers were dismissed. For example, who was a reserve captain or who was a reserve NCO or a reserve officer who did not want to go to Croatia, to the front line, they were dismissed. For example, Ramo Nalic went on working. He went to Croatia. Ahmed Alic also went on working but he went to the front line in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that in this factory in the autumn of 1991 there were more Muslims employed than Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you it is correct, but they were not in management positions or people who were reserve officers or non-commissioned officers and who did not want to go to the front line were dismissed. And other people were taken in who were not officers or NCOs. That's the way it was. And also at the mine, there were more Muslims working there than Serbs. However, all of those who were officers were dismissed, for the most part only because they were Muslims who did not want to go to the front line in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On page 6, paragraph 3, you say that radio Sana on the 26th of May, 1992, called on members of the Green Berets, even by name, to hand over their weapons. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you also know all these names? Did you remember them from the radio broadcast or are they names that are familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They're names that are familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were members of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, they weren't. And they didn't even have weapons. Let me tell you, Your Honours, Nihad Kljucanain's name, from the village of Trnovo, was read out. He was to bring back a gun from Trnovo. This gun belonged to the mosque, and do you know how big it was? The man brought it to the police station on his bicycle. And this man ended up in Manjaca. He could put it on his bicycle because it was used -- it was a bronze cannon which could be filled with gunpowder and lighted with a fuse, and this was to announce the end of Bajram, the Muslim holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've already had an additional seven minutes, Mr. Milosevic, above the time you should have had. You can have another five. That will give you approximately an hour and a half to cross-examine this witness, and that's more than enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, they read out names. I was referring to your statement. They read out names over radio Sana, members of the Green Berets, that is. Do you know that in 1991 the Patriotic League had 103 municipal staffs in 106 municipalities? That was the number that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, and Sefer Halilovic mentions this in his book.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not read Sefer Halilovic's books. I haven't read them. And secondly, I'm really not aware of this. I don't know that the Patriotic League existed in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As you say, there were no Green Berets, who, on the 27th of May, 1992, attacked the units of the army of Republika Srpska in the village of Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Hrustovo and Sanski Most are 15 kilometres apart, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who attacked them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The local villagers. In fact, they didn't attack them; I have to clarify this. The Yugoslav army blocked the village of Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, Kljevci, and they set out to kill civilians in these villages, but the local people did not hand over their weapons. Nobody was killed in the army, as far as I know, because the civilians who were armed and the civilian population, the women and children, withdrew to a wood called Golaja, and this is just what I heard. I didn't see this. The wood of Golaja is three kilometres away from Vrhpolje and from Hrustovo, but they entered the villages because they knew that some civilians, some of whom were armed, had withdrawn into the wood. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you don't know who attacked the units of Republika Srpska in Hrustovo. You don't even know about this attack; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one was killed, but I can't tell you what happened there because I wasn't there. This was 17 kilometres away. I wasn't there, I can't answer your question. I know that nobody was killed because had someone been killed, I have to tell you, Your Honours, I have to clarify this, the Serbs said on the radio if a single Serb soldier is killed, a hundred civilians will be shot. That's what they said on the radio. Because Dragan, who was a radio journalist, he commented on every battle as if it was a football game. When there was an attack on Sanski Most - I'm going backwards in time now - he said the Green Berets, the TO, they're attacking here, they're attacking there. He mentioned officers by name, saying who was shooting, from which firearm, from where, from which unit, which battery. And we listened to this when the attack began. We had to listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zulic. You say he commented on this as if it was a football game, reporting from where the Green Berets were attacking.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So were they the Green Berets or not?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to Mahala now. So wherever they said where the Green Berets were attacking, for example in the village of Skutsani Vakuf [phoen], the Green Berets were attacking, that's what they said. And we knew right away that that village would be attacked. Or Trnovo, for example, we knew the village would be attacked and burnt down, because when they were going to burn down Trnovo, they said there were Green Berets there. And then they brought in guns, tanks, and the whole village was razed to the ground. In 1995, there was not a stone left standing in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So were there attacks by the Green Berets or not? Was this journalist lying when he was commenting on these battles or did the things he was talking about actually happen?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, this was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And who attacked the units of the army of Republika Srpska near Vrhpolje on the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: First of all, I've already said that nobody attacked them. It was they who attacked. Not units of the Serbian army but units of the JNA. Not Serbian. Don't get this mixed up. The Serbian army operated after the JNA had done its work, because the JNA had a five-pointed star, and the paramilitary units later on looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the time you're speaking of, the army of Republika Srpska had already been established, which is why I'm asking you about attacks on the army.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, then they probably forgot to take off their five-pointed stars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe they didn't want to take them off.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you about that. You have to ask them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zulic, we won't go into that, but you said that somebody said on the radio that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This must be your last question. You've already gone over the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I think it's quite clear that if I'm questioning a witness who says that both his statements are not true, and this is the basis for my examination, I can't examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's well known from the Second World War that when the Germans actually shot a hundred hostages for one soldier who was killed, how can you ascribe this to the army of Republika Srpska or to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question for the witness. That's a purely argumentative point. No doubt if you want, you can make that Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 30025 to 30038. point to us in argument if it has any significance, but it's pure argument. It's not a proper question. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I'm going to ask you questions now about something that is in your transcript of your evidence from the previous time you gave evidence, your diary, and your statement that you made on the 14th of June, 2001, and it concerns the incident that happened when men had their throats slit. Do you understand? I'll ask you questions about each document in sequence, all right? If we just turn to the transcript now, at page 6908 in Exhibit 609, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need to put it before the witness because it will probably take too long in the sense of it. You described when you gave evidence in the trial on the 17th of June 2002, that the men had their throats slit, and then at a point when you were about to have your throat slit - I'm looking now at page 6910 - a voice you recognised said, "Simo, leave him alone." And that was a man called Rasula. And then a man came up to you and put a pistol in your mouth, and another man put a pistol to your head, and you thought the pistol was fired. Now, that evidence that you gave in the trial last year, was that an accurate account of what happened to you when you were describing the men having their throats slit by the grave?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: First of all this, was not on the 14th but on the 22nd of June. I spoke from memory. It's true that the gun was pushed into my mouth, and Your Honours, these teeth here are not my own, my front teeth. My teeth were broken. And they said they would baptise me. And then I recognised the name of -- the voice of a man who said they should let me go. I didn't say what Gojko Macura said to me, for example. I didn't say that because nobody asked me. Macura, that is Gojko Macura, also said that they had to leave me alone because they had to question me about weapons. I am simply adding this to what I said then. Because it will never be a pleasure for me to read my own diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just clarify one matter: Simo, who is referred to, there is a Simo Simetic. It appears that it may be him that the men were referring to, when they said, "Simo, leave him alone." Can you help us with that, Mr. Zulic? Who is Simo in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That Simo was a man who was a butcher. He was psychologically unbalanced even before the war. Even before the war he was not a stable personality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not Rasula, that's Simetic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us now turn to the diary which is in tab 3 of Exhibit 609, and I'm going to look here at page 7 in the English of the diary. And in that diary you describe about going to the place where you're given a hoe, and then you describe: "Macura put a pistol in my mouth." I'm looking at the sixth line down in English. "And Maunic against my forehead." Then a few lines further on you describe a shot, and then you go on to describe in the next paragraph, still on page 7, that Macura jerked the pistol out of your mouth, knocking your teeth loose. And then you go on further on that page, about two-thirds of the way down, that you realised the slaughter had begun because you heard a cry and a gurgling noise and a thud. And you describe Simo and the slitting of the throats. And then a voice said - and I'm turning now at the top of page 8 in the English - "Enough." And you go on to say about the eighth line down: "Enough for today." And you go on to say that something hit you in the back and you thought your turn had come, and you turned round, but you were taken away. Now, that order of events in your diary has, at the beginning, a pistol being put in your mouth and a throat being slit rather than what was said on the transcript of the throat slitting first and then the pistol being put in your mouth. Which is the correct order of events?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: When I'm responding to questions today, I may not be able to cover everything that's in my diary, because I haven't read my transcript. I tried to be as brief as possible when I was making my statements, and I tried to avoid pain as much as possible because you're taking me through the same thing that I experienced then, making me relive the experience. It's my duty to answer you. If I read the diary and my statement which you mentioned to me, I would probably -- if I had read this, I would probably have corrected it, but after writing my diary, I never reread it again, so that it's quite possibly -- it's quite possible that I recounted the events in the opposite sequence. I allow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's now then look at your statement on the 14th of June, 2001. And if we turn to page 10 of that statement, we deal with the same incident. In the second paragraph of the English version at page 10, you said: "They gave me a hoe," and you had to dig your own grave. And in the next paragraph you describe digging, and then in the second to last paragraph, which begins, "When I finished digging the hole, I had to stand up in front of the hole facing it." You heard screaming and shouting, and then you described Simo Simetic, the butcher, slitting the throats of the men by the grave. And you go on to say, "When it was my turn, he put his knife under my chin and held it there. He was moving it a little bit in order to cut my skin. I began to bleed." And then you describe Macura coming up to you, forcing open your mouth, putting the gun inside, and pulling it out and breaking your teeth. And then he put his gun to your forehead, and he shot a bullet through your hair. This is another different account of the same incident. When you described making earlier statements, to Mr. Milosevic's first questions, you indicated that this statement was false. Why have you given different versions of this incident in the transcript, the diary, and your statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that the transcript from the trial was a false statement, or this one. What I said was that I gave our police those statements. I didn't say that the transcript from the trial and this statement were false. I said that it was possible that I had said something - how shall I put this? - because I did not reread my diary. When you make a statement after ten years have elapsed, it cannot be a hundred per cent correct because it's very different when ten or 11 years have elapsed. Today when I talk about it, I will certainly not remember many details of what I lived through. That's the only difference, Your Honours. Because a person who goes through something like this loses his concentration very quickly, and you start trembling. You simply -- simply -- you can't concentrate. I can no longer concentrate because he tried to make me relive what I had gone through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it correct of you to have said in your statement to the Prosecution that your throat was bleeding because the knife had been drawn across your throat?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you please close this session and I will show the gentleman some things that are still visible today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will accept that they are visible. Mr. Kay, I don't think we can take this very much further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Perhaps it should be the case, though, that the statement of the 14th of June should be exhibited as a supplementary part of the 609, as well as the other statement to the Bosnian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be added to tab 12 of Prosecution Exhibit 609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I would just like to ask you a couple of questions just to clarify some confusion which may have arisen regarding the various statements which you gave. Now, they've been exhibited at tab 12. Can I kindly ask you to look at the statement which you gave to the Bosnian police, which I believe is already before you. Now, that is the statement which --

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And have Your Honours got this one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've got a copy, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: This is a statement which you earlier said was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of the session I showed you a piece of paper which has been exhibited at the back - if we could kindly also show the witness this - showing two corrections which you made regarding the fact that you were examined by the Red Cross rather than a doctor and that you were beaten in stables rather than a room. Now, apart from those two corrections, is, generally speaking, your statement before you otherwise correct? Taking into account it might not contain everything which you experienced which you've told us you didn't cover.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: A small part is correct. I wasn't examined by these doctors but by a doctor from the International Red Cross, and you can check this because I have my camp card and there's a number on it, and you can check this in Geneva, that I was examined by that doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, is this statement correct or is it incorrect? Because there seems to be some confusion. That statement which you're now looking at,.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this, Your Honours, is the one that he gave to the ICTY on the 14th of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have to read it all?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: No, no. All I'm asking you is, in essence, that statement there in general a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to clarify on the statements, because there seems to be some misunderstanding. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. What is it, Mr. Milosevic? We really need to get on with this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. The witness asked whether he had to read it all or not so that he could say whether it was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course he doesn't have to waste time reading it all. He asked -- answered that it was generally correct. Now, let us get on with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Just moving away from the question of your statements now. You mentioned in your answers to the accused, and you were very clear about this, is that the Serb people fled, they were not expelled from Sanski Most. In which year was this that they fled?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And why did they flee?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which liberated Kljuc-Petrovac, and so they fled together with their soldiers, they left with their military. Why they left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Was it an armed fight or was it against civilian people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: From Sanski Most, I'm saying about civilians, that they fled. The civilians fled from Sanski Most. At the time, there was no fighting between the armies in Sanski Most. From what I heard, because I wasn't there at the time, there was Seselj's men, Arkan's men. I heard they had headquarters in the local community house of the local commune of Pobrijezje. And when Kljuc and Petrovac were liberated by the Muslim army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which arrived to Palanka, the civilians pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, what crimes, if any, were Arkan's men committing in Sanski Most in 1995, who you just mentioned pulled out or fled?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, but I know that 18 people were taken away from my village by Arkan's men with the help of Pero Gavran who told them which houses were Serb and which houses were Muslim. They came into the village, picked up those people from their homes, and executed them somewhere between Sehovci and Sasina. These people were not only from Pobrijezje but from surrounding villages like Sasina. They needed some people for labour tasks, and they later executed the men after releasing women and children. They later transported women and children on to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: No further questions. That completes the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, that concludes your evidence. I'm sorry, there's a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, when the accused asked the question in the first part, he asked about whether you were telling the truth when you made the two statements, one to the Bosnian police and one to the ICTY investigators. I'm looking at the transcript. I'll quote the question: "Q. Were you telling the truth in both statements?" You said: "A. No. "Q. In which statement did you tell the truth and which didn't you?" And your answer: "A. I didn't tell the truth in any of them." And you state the reasons in private session, and during which you said that you didn't tell the truth to The Hague investigators. Is it a mistake or could you clarify this matter to us.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think that it must be a mistake, because I told the truth to the investigators of the ICTY, but I gave two other statements to our police force. But I can't say it any more in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's enough --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That's why it seems -- that's why it may appear that I did not tell the truth in either of the statements I gave to our police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what is incorrect is corrected by your addendum to the ICTY attorneys; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, Mr. Zulic. As I said, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt but there is actually a matter that I didn't deal with and Ms. Wee has kindly brought to my attention, and that is that the handwritten diaries were all disclosed on the 1st of June, 2002, so they ought to have been in the accused's possession. I apologise for not having dealt with that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with the next witness. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution will call Witness B-1021.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there a matter you have to raise first or do I have the wrong witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There is a point of clarification, Your Honour, thank you, and if possible, could we please go into private session because it deals with witness protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness will be closed session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
